question: Assume today is 2026-08-23. You know nothing published after this date. Estimate the number of live births in South Korea in July 2026, as it will be first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release.

target.what: Number of live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported in the national statistics agency's monthly Population Trends release
target.cadence: monthly, typically released around the last week of the second following month (e.g., July data released late September 2026)
target.caveats: The target period is completed relative to the 2026-08-23 cutoff, but the official July 2026 figure is not yet published. The first report may be provisional and subject to revision. Live births are counted by date of occurrence, not registration date; late registration can cause small revisions. Th

candidates.hypothesis: The July 2026 count can be projected from the same month in prior years, adjusted for trend and seasonality. July typically shows a seasonal pattern relative to adjacent months; recent year-over-year changes in monthly births provide a base for extrapolation.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly live birth counts for South Korea from January 2023 through June 2026 (the latest available before cutoff), with July values for 2023, 2024, and 2025. Also monthly year-over-year percent changes for 2025 and 2026 year-to-date. If the full series is unavailable, at least July 2023–2025 and the most recent 12 months.
search_hints: South Korea monthly birth data July 2025

candidates.hypothesis: Births are registered with local governments, and the number of birth registrations in a month is closely related to the number of live births occurring in that month, though with a lag. If registration data for July 2026 are available before the KOSTAT release, they can provide an early indicator.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly birth registration counts from the Ministry of the Interior and Safety (행정안전부) resident registration system for July 2026, or weekly/daily registration counts for July 2026. Also the historical relationship between registration counts and KOSTAT live birth counts (e.g., ratio or lag).

candidates.hypothesis: Most births occur in hospitals, and health insurance claims for delivery-related care can serve as a proxy for live births. The number of claims for normal delivery or cesarean section in July 2026, if available, can be scaled to national births.
candidates.data_to_find: National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) or Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service (HIRA) statistics on delivery-related claims for July 2026, or monthly counts of childbirth-related medical care. Also the historical ratio of such claims to KOSTAT live births.

candidates.hypothesis: The number of live births is constrained by the number of obstetric beds, delivery rooms, and obstetricians, and their utilisation. If capacity and utilisation data for July 2026 are available, they can bound the plausible number of births.
candidates.data_to_find: Number of obstetric beds and delivery rooms in South Korea, average occupancy rate or deliveries per obstetrician per month, and any July 2026 utilisation data from hospitals or the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service. Also the number of active obstetricians in July 2026.

candidates.hypothesis: Births in July 2026 may be affected by the timing of holidays, government incentives, or changes in parental leave policies. For example, if a new birth incentive was introduced in 2025 or 2026, it could have shifted birth timing. Also, the Lunar calendar and school entry cutoff can influence seasonality.
candidates.data_to_find: Any policy changes in 2025–2026 related to childbirth incentives, parental leave, or baby bonuses; the exact dates of implementation; and evidence of their impact on monthly birth counts in prior months. Also the number of weekdays and weekends in July 2026 compared to July 2025.

candidates.hypothesis: Statistics Korea or other institutions may publish monthly or quarterly birth projections that include July 2026. These can serve as a prior, though they may be model-based rather than observed.
candidates.data_to_find: Any published monthly birth forecasts for 2026 from Statistics Korea, Bank of Korea, or research institutes; also any nowcasting reports for July 2026 births. Check for release dates before 2026-08-23.

candidates.hypothesis: Live births in a month can be estimated from the number of women of childbearing age and the general fertility rate, or from the number of marriages in prior months (since first births often follow marriage). If marriage counts for late 2025 and early 2026 are available, they can inform births in July 2026.
candidates.data_to_find: Monthly marriage counts in South Korea from January 2025 to June 2026, and the historical lag between marriage and first birth. Also the number of women aged 20–39 in 2026 and age-specific fertility rates.

candidates.hypothesis: Public interest in pregnancy and childbirth, as measured by search volume or media coverage, may correlate with birth numbers, but the link is weak and lagged. This can provide a qualitative check on whether July 2026 births are likely above or below trend.
candidates.data_to_find: Google Trends or Naver DataLab search volumes for terms like '임신', '출산', '아기' for July 2026, and any news articles about a baby boom or decline in mid-2026. Compare to previous years.

p3.role: number of clinic/hospital-level obstetric-gynecology facilities providing delivery care nationwide in South Korea in 2025

a1.role: annual live births per delivery-capable clinic/hospital-level facility

a2.role: July share of annual live births

methods.rationale: Capacity-times-throughput decomposition: the 2025 stock of delivery-capable clinic/hospital-level facilities (p3) times an assumed average annual births per facility (a1) gives an annual national birth flow, and times the July share (a2) gives July 2026. This is a physical-flow route, not a claim that capacity equals output; a1 is the bridge from capacity to realised births. Main failure modes: a1 is weakly identified because deliveries are concentrated in large hospitals not counted in p3, and the 2025 facility stock may not hold in July 2026. Shared dependency: p3 also underlies the scope comparison with p5.

p3.role: number of clinic/hospital-level obstetric-gynecology facilities providing delivery care nationwide in South Korea in 2025

a1.role: annual live births per delivery-capable clinic/hospital-level facility

a2.role: July share of annual live births

a3.role: year-over-year change factor for July 2026 relative to the 2025-based level

methods.rationale: Same capacity-times-throughput route as m1 but with an explicit year-over-year change factor (a3) to allow for the 2025-to-2026 trend. This is a scenario-style variant rather than an independent measurement; it shares p3, a1 and a2 with m1, so agreement between m1 and m2 is not independent confirmation. It is included only to show sensitivity to the trend assumption; if a July 2025 observed level becomes available (b2), this route should be replaced by a direct analogue method.

assumptions.name: Annual live births per delivery-capable clinic/hospital-level facility
assumptions.unit: live births per facility per year
assumptions.rationale: No kept point gives a births-per-facility rate. With roughly 230,000-250,000 annual births in South Korea in the mid-2020s and 260 clinic/hospital-level delivery providers (p3), the implied average is about 900-960 births per facility per year; tertiary/general hospitals handle a large share of deliveries, so the clinic/hospital-level average is plausibly lower. A central value of 700 with a wide 350-1400 range reflects this and the strong concentration of deliveries in a few large hospitals.
assumptions.applies_when: Used only to convert the 2025 stock of delivery-capable clinic/hospital-level facilities (p3) into an annual birth flow; assumes the 2025 facility stock and average throughput carry into July 2026.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that the number of delivery-capable facilities changed materially in 2026, or a published births-per-facility rate outside 350-1400.

assumptions.name: July share of annual live births
assumptions.rationale: July is one of 12 months; Korean birth seasonality is mild, with a modest autumn peak and a slightly below-average summer. A share near 1/12 (0.0833) with a narrow range is appropriate; no kept point supplies monthly seasonality, so this is an explicit assumption.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to convert an annual birth flow into the July 2026 target period; assumes seasonality in 2026 resembles the recent historical pattern.
assumptions.falsified_by: Published monthly birth shares showing July materially outside 7.8-8.8% of the annual total.

assumptions.name: Year-over-year change factor for July 2026 vs July 2025
assumptions.rationale: Korean births have been declining but showed signs of stabilisation in 2024-2025; absent a published July 2026 figure, a central no-change factor with a +/-10% range is honest. This is a change factor relative to an observed earlier period, not a level of the target.
assumptions.applies_when: Used to carry a July 2025 analogue level forward to July 2026; requires a kept July 2025 birth level, which is currently missing (see b2).
assumptions.falsified_by: Registration or vital-statistics data showing July 2026 births more than 10% above or below July 2025.

assessment.note: Both count the same universe (all ob/gyn clinics and hospitals nationwide) in 2021 and 2025; the near-identical totals (1,573 vs 1,571) show the stock of ob/gyn facilities is essentially flat, so facility counts alone carry almost no signal about birth volume.

p3/p4 (260 facilities, 16.5% of 1,571) and the p9-p12 series (313→300→282→269→260) are the same measurement of clinic/hospital-level delivery providers from the same article; p3 is the 2025 endpoint of the p9-p12 series, so they are not independent observations.
All four describe the same broader delivery-provider universe (436 in 2025 vs 620 in 2015, a 184-facility / 29.7% decline); p7 and p8 are arithmetic restatements of p5 and p6, not separate evidence.

Different but nested scopes: 260 clinic/hospital-level providers (p3) versus 436 including tertiary and general hospitals and midwifery clinics (p5). They are consistent (p3 < p5) and together define the capacity envelope, but neither is a birth count.

Seoul-specific pair from the same article: 437 ob/gyn facilities, only 41 doing deliveries. Consistent with the national pattern of a small delivery-active share; useful only as a geographic concentration check.
Same July 2025 marriage release: 20,394 marriages and +8.4% year-over-year. The level and the change are one measurement, not two.
Same July 2025 divorce release: 7,826 divorces and -1.4% year-over-year; one measurement.

All three come from the same KOSTAT July 2025 Population Trends release (published 2025-09-24), so they share a source and vintage; they establish the release cadence and the July-2025 marriage level but contain no birth count.

One consistent cohort series of mean marriage-to-first-birth intervals (15.0→16.7 months, 2015→2020 cohorts) from a single 2022 release; the trend is monotone and slow, so extrapolation to 2025-2026 marriages is a mild extension.
One consistent cohort series of first-to-second-birth intervals (24.8→23.8 months); same source and vintage as p25-p30.
Dual-income (17.2 months) vs single-income (16.3 months) first-birth intervals for the 2020 cohort; same release, and the gap is small relative to the overall spread.

Both from the same 2020-cohort newlywed analysis: p25 gives the mean interval for couples with children, p38 shows only 55.5% of newlywed couples had a child within 5 years. Together they warn that marriage counts map to births with both a lag and a large non-conversion share.

First-birth lag (~16.7 months) and second-birth lag (~23.8 months) are different parity transitions; they cannot be averaged into a single marriage-to-birth lag without a parity mix, which no kept point supplies.

p3.role: Number of clinic/hospital-level ob/gyn facilities actually providing delivery care nationwide in South Korea, 2025 (capacity base for July 2026)

a1.role: Live births per delivery-active clinic/hospital-level facility per month in South Korea, July 2026

methods.rationale: Capacity-times-throughput decomposition. p3 gives the observed 2025 stock of clinic/hospital-level delivery providers (260), which is the only kept point that measures delivery-active capacity directly; a1 converts that stock into a monthly birth flow. This route deliberately excludes the ~176 tertiary/general/midwifery institutions in p5, so it is a lower-tier estimate rather than a full national total; the wide a1 range is intended to absorb both the unobserved throughput and the omitted upper tier. Shared dependency: both m1 and m2 ultimately rest on the same unobserved 2026 birth level, so they are not independent confirmations. Failure mode: if deliveries have concentrated further into large hospitals since 2025, p3-based capacity understates the flow and a1 would need to be higher.

p_july2025_births.role: PLACEHOLDER — see rationale; no kept point supplies the July 2025 live-birth level, so this route cannot be executed with the current library

a2.role: Ratio of July 2026 live births to July 2025 live births, South Korea

methods.rationale: Trend-transfer route: take the July 2025 KOSTAT live-birth level and apply a marriage-driven change factor (a2). This is the most direct analogue route and would be preferred if the base level were available. It is NOT executable with the current library: no kept point reports the July 2025 (or any 2024/2025) live-birth count — the July 2025 Population Trends release points in the library cover deaths (p19), marriages (p20) and divorces (p22) only. The placeholder input id above is not a real data-point id and must not be treated as one; the specific missing input is the KOSTAT monthly live-birth level for July 2025 (or an equivalent recent July). Targeted repair: retrieve the July 2025 live-birth figure from the same KOSTAT release vintage as p19-p23, or the resident-registration birth count for July 2026 (direction b1), which would also unlock a direct level route. Until then this method should be dropped rather than approximated.

assumptions.name: Live births per delivery-active clinic/hospital-level ob/gyn facility per month, South Korea, July 2026
assumptions.unit: live births per facility per month
assumptions.rationale: No kept point gives a births-per-facility throughput. The value is anchored on the scale implied by the capacity envelope: 260 clinic/hospital-level delivery providers (p3) and 436 total delivery institutions (p5) must jointly accommodate a national monthly birth flow that has been in the low tens of thousands. A central value of ~55 births per clinic/hospital-level facility per month implies roughly 14,000 births/month from this tier, leaving the remainder to the ~176 tertiary/general/midwifery institutions in p5, which is consistent with the known concentration of deliveries in larger hospitals. The range is deliberately wide because facility-level throughput is unobserved and highly skewed (large hospitals deliver far more than small clinics).
assumptions.applies_when: The 2025 facility stock (p3, p5) is still representative of July 2026 capacity and utilisation, and the delivery-active facility mix has not shifted materially in the intervening year.
assumptions.falsified_by: Evidence that the number of delivery-active facilities changed sharply in 2026, or any observed monthly birth count for 2025-2026 that implies a births-per-facility throughput far outside 30-100.

assumptions.name: Ratio of July 2026 live births to July 2025 live births, South Korea
assumptions.rationale: The only kept evidence on the recent direction of births is indirect: marriages in July 2025 were 20,394, up 8.4% year-over-year (p20), and the marriage-to-first-birth lag is about 16-17 months (p25), so the late-2024/2025 marriage recovery should begin feeding into births around mid-2026. However, only about 55.5% of newlywed couples have a child within five years (p38), so the marriage-to-birth pass-through is far below one-for-one. A modest positive ratio with a wide band reflects this partial pass-through and the possibility that the marriage uptick is offset by continued fertility-rate decline.
assumptions.applies_when: The July 2025 KOSTAT live-birth level is available as the base period and the marriage-to-birth transmission observed in p20/p25/p38 is the dominant driver of the 2025-to-2026 change.
assumptions.falsified_by: A published July 2026 birth count, or 2026 monthly birth data, showing a change outside the 0.95-1.12 band, or evidence that the 2025 marriage increase did not translate into first births.

kept.name: Live births per delivery-active clinic/hospital-level ob/gyn facility per month, South Korea, July 2026
kept.unit: live births per facility per month
kept.rationale: No kept point gives a births-per-facility throughput. The value is anchored on the scale implied by the capacity envelope: 260 clinic/hospital-level delivery providers (p3) and 436 total delivery institutions (p5) must jointly accommodate a national monthly birth flow that has been in the low tens o
kept.applies_when: The 2025 facility stock (p3, p5) is still representative of July 2026 capacity and utilisation, and the delivery-active facility mix has not shifted materially in the intervening year.
kept.falsified_by: Evidence that the number of delivery-active facilities changed sharply in 2026, or any observed monthly birth count for 2025-2026 that implies a births-per-facility throughput far outside 30-100.

kept.name: Ratio of July 2026 live births to July 2025 live births, South Korea
kept.rationale: The only kept evidence on the recent direction of births is indirect: marriages in July 2025 were 20,394, up 8.4% year-over-year (p20), and the marriage-to-first-birth lag is about 16-17 months (p25), so the late-2024/2025 marriage recovery should begin feeding into births around mid-2026. However,
kept.applies_when: The July 2025 KOSTAT live-birth level is available as the base period and the marriage-to-birth transmission observed in p20/p25/p38 is the dominant driver of the 2025-to-2026 change.
kept.falsified_by: A published July 2026 birth count, or 2026 monthly birth data, showing a change outside the 0.95-1.12 band, or evidence that the 2025 marriage increase did not translate into first births.

final.template:
The best computed estimate for live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported by Statistics Korea's Monthly Population Trends, is [[estimate]] ([[interval_level]] interval [[p10]] to [[p90]], [[interval_basis]]). The estimate rests on [[n_points_kept]] observed point and [[n_methods]] method, weighted [[m1_weight]]. The only observed input is the stock of delivery-active clinic/hospital-level ob/gyn facilities; the births-per-facility throughput of [[a1_value]] (range [[a1_low]] to [[a1_high]]) is an analyst assumption, not observed. This route deliberately excludes tertiary and midwifery institutions, so it is a lower-tier capacity estimate rather than a full national count. The interval is model-based and conditional on that assumption, not a demonstrated accuracy guarantee. The result could be wrong mainly because the throughput assumption is unanchored and facility counts may not map cleanly to monthly birth flow. The missing evidence that would most improve it is an observed births-per-facility throughput series or a directly reported monthly birth count.

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 Live births per delivery-active clinic/hospital-level ob/gyn facility per month, South Korea, July 2026: [[a1_value]] live births per facility per month, range [[a1_low]] to [[a1_high]]; used by m1. Overturned by: Evidence that the number of delivery-active facilities changed sharply in 2026, or any observed monthly birth count for 2025-2026 that implies a births-per-facility throughput far outside [n]-[n].
final.text:
The best computed estimate for live births occurring in South Korea during July 2026, as first reported by Statistics Korea's Monthly Population Trends, is 14,229 (80% interval 7,568 to 26,756, monte carlo). The estimate rests on 14 observed point and 1 method, weighted 100%. The only observed input is the stock of delivery-active clinic/hospital-level ob/gyn facilities; the births-per-facility throughput of 55 (range 30 to 100) is an analyst assumption, not observed. This route deliberately excludes tertiary and midwifery institutions, so it is a lower-tier capacity estimate rather than a full national count. The interval is model-based and conditional on that assumption, not a demonstrated accuracy guarantee. The result could be wrong mainly because the throughput assumption is unanchored and facility counts may not map cleanly to monthly birth flow. The missing evidence that would most improve it is an observed births-per-facility throughput series or a directly reported monthly birth count.

Key assumptions (proposed by the analyst model, not observed; code samples each one between the bounds shown):
- a1 Live births per delivery-active clinic/hospital-level ob/gyn facility per month, South Korea, July 2026: 55 live births per facility per month, range 30 to 100; used by m1. Overturned by: Evidence that the number of delivery-active facilities changed sharply in 2026, or any observed monthly birth count for 2025-2026 that implies a births-per-facility throughput far outside [n]-[n].

searcher_queries_containing_registered_v: Korea births July 2026 monthly population trends 24,275
by_construction: Only URLs leave the searcher (code regex); extractor, judge and final prompts never contain search result titles, snippets or the searcher's text. This holds by construction and is not measured.
residual_risks: The searcher sees post-cutoff search results and chooses which URLs are fetched, so page selection can be conditioned on the answer; only the URLs leave the searcher, and in backtests every fetched page is a snapshot dated <= as_of.
Live pages are used only when as_of is today; in backtests every page is an archived snapshot dated <= as_of.
The leak sentinel only catches registered official values in common formats, not paraphrased or derived numbers.
The model's own training data (knowledge cutoff unpublished) can include history before as_of; it cannot include the target if the target was published after the model's release.
Wayback snapshots are captured by a third party; a snapshot date <= as_of proves the content existed by then.
Assumption values are proposed by the judge model from its own knowledge, which can include the target's history before as_of; code checks their form, not where the number came from.

ablation.rule: exclude points from own_history directions and points whose name contains a target entity anchor and whose name or unit shares a stem with the target unit (triangulate/agent/ablation.py)
residual_risks: Own values named by an alias or abbreviation, or with no entity in the point name, are not excluded.

The rule over-excludes on purpose: any point naming the target entity together with the target quantity (for example a survey of the target's visitors) is excluded, even when it is not a value of the target itself.
The model's own memory of the target's history is not removed: it can still shape the plan, the judge's choices and assumption values.
The searcher and the extractor still see pages that contain own values; only the judge's table is filtered.
